result.relation_rationale: The selected result exactly matches the requested Overall Survival comparison: individually randomized men assigned to ADT alone or ADT plus abiraterone acetate and prednisolone; overall survival is time from randomization to death from any cause; the efficacy analysis included all patients under intention-to-treat.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

For each active question, review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires a Trial-scoped, untruncated search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. The server checks structure and Evidence identity; you judge whether the cited facts support the answer.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If you cannot reliably resolve the complete active path, answer each question on that active path using an allowed official answer value and supported bases. Submit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.

questions.wording: Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomization process?
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 17-18, Box 4, signalling question 1.3
questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison

data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
nation therapy against control for survival could
be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
stopping guidelines.
Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median
duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
Results
Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.
Treatment
The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the
initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
clined treatment. The median duration of abira
terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
continue through progression (51% reported per-
manent stopping for progression and 20% for
excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
report.
The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
therapy was 39% in the combination group and
40% in the ADT-alone group.

There were 184 deaths in the combination group
and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
combination group, with a 3-year survival of
83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

BACKGROUND
Abiraterone acetate plus prednisolone improves survival in men with relapsed pros-
tate cancer. We assessed the effect of this combination in men starting long-term
androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT), using a multigroup, multistage trial design.
METHODS
We randomly assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to receive ADT alone or ADT plus abir
aterone acetate (1000 mg daily) and prednisolone (5 mg daily) (combination therapy).
Local radiotherapy was mandated for patients with node-negative, nonmetastatic
disease and encouraged for those with positive nodes. For patients with nonmeta-
static disease with no radiotherapy planned and for patients with metastatic disease,
treatment continued until radiologic, clinical, or prostate-specific antigen (PSA) pro-
gression; otherwise, treatment was to continue for 2 years or until any type of progres-
sion, whichever came first. The primary outcome measure was overall survival. The
intermediate primary outcome was failure-free survival (treatment failure was de-
fined as radiologic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from prostate cancer).
RESULTS
A total of 1917 patients underwent randomization from November 2011 through
January 2014. The median age was 67 years, and the median PSA level was 53 ng per
milliliter. A total of 52% of the patients had metastatic disease, 20% had node-positive
or node-indeterminate nonmetastatic disease, and 28% had node-negative, nonmeta-
static disease; 95% had newly diagnosed disease. The median follow-up was 40
months. There were 184 deaths in the combination group as compared with 262 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76;
P<0.001); the hazard ratio was 0.75 in patients with nonmetastatic disease and 0.61
in those with metastatic disease. There were 248 treatment-failure events in the
combination group as compared with 535 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001); the hazard ratio was 0.21 in patients with non-
metastatic disease and 0.31 in those with metastatic disease. Grade 3 to 5 adverse
events occurred in 47% of the patients in the combination group (with nine grade 5
events) and in 33% of the patients in the ADT-alone group (with three grade 5 events).
CONCLUSIONS
Among men with locally advanced or metastatic prostate cancer, ADT plus abiraterone
and prednisolone was associated with significantly higher rates of overall and
failure-free survival than ADT alone. (Funded by Cancer Research U.K. and others;
STAMPEDE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00268476, and Current Controlled Trials
number, ISRCTN78818544.)

4|T
5|he Systemic Therapy in Advancing
6|or Metastatic Prostate Cancer: Evaluation
7|of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE) trial recruits
8|patients commencing long-term androgen-depri-
9|vation therapy (ADT; orchiectomy or gonadotropin-
10|releasing hormone [GnRH] agonists or antago-
11|nists) for the first time for locally advanced or
12|metastatic prostate cancer. Several agents have
13|improved overall survival (docetaxel, abiraterone
14|acetate, enzalutamide, cabazitaxel, radium-223,
15|and sipuleucel-T)1-8 or reduced morbidity (zole-
16|dronic acid and denosumab)9-11 among such pa-
17|tients. These agents were initially investigated in
18|men with very advanced disease whose tumors
19|had progressed during first-line ADT, a disease
20|state now termed castration-resistant prostate
21|cancer.
22|The STAMPEDE trial uses a novel multigroup,
23|multistage (also called multiarm, multistage
24|[MAMS]) platform design12-14 to test whether the
25|addition of further treatments to ADT improves
26|overall survival if used in the first-line setting. It
27|uses intermediate activity analyses, based on
28|failure-free survival, to cease randomization to
29|research groups that are insufficiently active.12-14
30|We have previously reported that treatment with
31|docetaxel at the inception of ADT increased me-
32|dian survival from 71 months to 81 months as
33|well as overall survival (hazard ratio for death,
34|0.76).15,16 These results, along with those of a
35|systematic review that included other trials17-19
36|and of a meta-analysis,16 led to docetaxel becom-
37|ing a part of the standard of care for suitable
38|patients with prostate cancer who had not re-
39|ceived previous hormone therapy.
40|An important mechanism for escape from
41|tumor control by androgen ablation includes the
42|intracellular conversion of steroid precursors to
43|androgenic steroids by prostate-cancer cells.
44|Abiraterone acetate is a selective, irreversible in-
45|hibitor of CYP17, an enzyme that is critical in the
46|production of androgens in the testes, adrenal
47|glands, and prostate-tumor tissue. Inhibition of
48|CYP17 in combination with ADT results in a
49|more effective androgen depletion than can be
50|induced by surgical castration or by GnRH ana-
51|logues alone.20 Two large, phase 3 trials showed
52|that the addition of abiraterone acetate with pred-
53|nisolone to standard-of-care therapy prolonged
54|survival among men with castration-resistant
55|prostate cancer.4,5,21 The STAMPEDE trial is inves-
56|tigating whether the earlier use of abiraterone in
57|men who are initiating long-term ADT could
58|improve survival.
59|Methods
60|Trial Design and Patients
61|We used a multigroup, multistage platform de-
62|sign, incorporating a seamless phase 2-3 com-
63|ponent. The primary outcome was overall sur-
64|vival, defined as the time from randomization to
65|death from any cause. The intermediate primary
66|outcome was failure-free survival, defined as the
67|time to the first of the following forms of treat-
68|ment failure: biochemical (prostate-specific anti-
69|gen [PSA]) failure (see the protocol, available
70|with the full text of this article at NEJM.org);
71|progression of local, lymph-node, or distant
72|metastases; or death from prostate cancer. Second
73|ary outcome measures included adverse events,
74|symptomatic skeletal events, progression-free
75|survival (i.e., failure-free survival excluding bio-
76|chemical failure), prostate cancer-specific sur-
77|vival, and (data not shown) quality of life.
78|The rationale and design were described pre-
79|viously.12-14,22 Full details are provided in the pro-
80|tocol. In summary, eligible patients had prostate
81|cancer that was newly diagnosed and metastatic,
82|node-positive, or high-risk locally advanced (with
83|at least two of following: a tumor stage of T3 or
84|T4, a Gleason score of 8 to 10, and a PSA level
85|≥40 ng per milliliter) or disease that was previ-
86|ously treated with radical surgery or radiother
87|apy and was now relapsing with high-risk fea-
88|tures (in men no longer receiving therapy, a PSA
89|level >4 ng per milliliter with a doubling time of
90|<6 months, a PSA level >20 ng per milliliter,
91|nodal or metastatic relapse, or <12 months of
92|total ADT with an interval of >12 months with-
93|out treatment). Patients were intended for treat-
94|ment with long-term ADT that started no longer
95|than 12 weeks before randomization. There were
96|no age restrictions. Patients with clinically sig-
97|nificant cardiovascular disease (e.g., severe angi-
98|na, recent myocardial infarction, or a history of
99|cardiac failure) were excluded.

102|Research Council (MRC) and conducted by the

14|tion. Representatives from Janssen were invited
15|to comment on the manuscript. Further funding
16|for the platform was provided by Astellas Pharma,
17|Clovis Oncology, Novartis, Pfizer, and Sanofi
18|Aventis. The trial was conducted in accordance
19|with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
20|guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki, and
21|the appropriate regulatory and ethics approvals
22|were obtained. All the patients provided written
23|informed consent.
24|The analyses were driven by prespecified cri-
25|teria, and the decision to submit the manuscript
26|for publication was made by the members of the
27|Trial Management Group. Three authors at the
28|MRC Clinical Trials Unit at UCL accessed the raw
29|data; processed data that were released by the
30|independent data monitoring committee and trial
31|steering committee were available to all the co-
32|authors. The authors vouch for the completeness
33|and accuracy of the data and analyses and for the
34|adherence of the trial to the protocol. No one
35|who is not an author contributed to the writing
36|of the manuscript.
37|Randomization and Masking
38|Randomization was performed centrally by tele-
39|phone with the use of a computerized algorithm,
40|which was developed and maintained by the MRC
41|Clinical Trials Unit at UCL. Minimization with a
42|random element of 80% was used, with stratifi-
43|cation according to randomizing center, age at
44|randomization (<70 vs. ≥70 years), the presence
45|or absence of metastases, planned use of pros-
46|tate radiotherapy (yes vs. no), nodal involvement
47|(negative vs. indeterminate vs. positive), World
48|Health Organization performance status (0 vs.
49|1 or 2 [on a scale of 0 to 4, with higher numbers
50|indicating greater disability]), type of ADT, and
51|regular, long-term use of aspirin or nonsteroidal
52|antiinflammatory drugs (yes vs. no). The assign-
53|ment ratio was 1:1 to standard of care alone or
54|with abiraterone acetate and prednisolone (combi-
55|nation therapy). The comparison was open-label,
56|because masking of the treatment assignment
57|was deemed impracticable. Eligible patients could
58|be assigned to any of the trial groups that were
59|open; we focus here on patients assigned con-
60|temporaneously to ADT alone or with abiraterone
61|and prednisolone.
62|Procedures
63|ADT was given for at least 2 years; radiotherapy
64|at 6 to 9 months after randomization was man-
65|datory for patients with node-negative, nonmeta-
66|static disease and optional for patients with node-
67|positive, nonmetastatic disease. Abiraterone
68|(1000 mg) with prednisolone (5 mg) was given
69|once daily. The treatment duration depended on
70|disease stage and intent for radical radiotherapy:
71|for patients with nonmetastatic disease with no
72|radiotherapy planned and for patients with meta-
73|static disease, treatment continued until PSA,
74|radiologic, or clinical progression or until an-
75|other treatment was started; for patients with
76|nonmetastatic disease with radiotherapy planned,
77|treatment was to continue for 2 years or until
78|any type of progression, whichever came first.
79|Dose modifications are described in the protocol.
80|Patients were assessed every 6 weeks during
81|the first 6 months, then every 12 weeks until
82|2 years, then every 6 months until 5 years, and
83|then annually; in addition, patients receiving
84|combination therapy were assessed at least every
85|3 months. Assessments included PSA testing and
86|ascertainment of adverse events; further tests
87|were conducted at the discretion of the treating
88|physician. The nadir PSA level (for the definition
89|of PSA progression) was defined as the lowest
90|level within 24 weeks after randomization. There
91|was no protocol-mandated imaging except at
92|baseline. Adverse events were assessed with the
93|use of the National Cancer Institute Common
94|Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (initial-
95|ly, version 3.0; later, version 4.0). Serious adverse
96|events and reactions were reported accordingly.
97|Statistical Analysis
98|The sample size was calculated with the use of
99|Stata nstage and predecessor programs that allow
100|for the design of multigroup, multistage trials.23
101|Assuming a median failure-free survival of 2 years
102|and a median overall survival between 4 and
103|5 years for ADT, we targeted a 25% relative dif-

4|ADT-alone group for both failure-free survival
5|(hazard ratio for treatment failure, 0.75) and
6|overall survival (hazard ratio for death, 0.75).
7|The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
8|nation therapy against control for survival could
9|be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
10|mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
11|power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
12|we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
13|benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
14|pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
15|accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
16|stopping guidelines.
17|Data on patients without an event of interest
18|were censored when they were last known to be
19|event-free. The median follow-up was determined
20|through reversing death and censoring indica-
21|tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
22|used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
23|ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
24|for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
25|models to estimate relative treatment effects.
26|These estimates were adjusted for stratification
27|factors (except randomizing center and ADT
28|method) and were stratified according to time
29|periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
30|ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
31|group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
32|ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
33|parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
34|proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
35|restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
36|the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
37|fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
38|fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
39|of treatment effect according to stratification
40|factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
41|and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
42|before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
43|group analyses according to metastatic status
44|were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
45|prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
46|free survival according to the age at random-
47|ization.
48|All the patients were included in the efficacy
49|analyses under their assigned treatment on an
50|intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
51|tients were grouped according to the treatment
52|that they started. In the analysis of the median
53|duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
54|sored at the date of last contact with the patient
55|if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
56|Results
57|Patients
58|Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
59|2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
60|U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
61|(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
62|therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
63|The flow of patients through the trial is shown
64|in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
65|available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
66|tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
67|Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
68|median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
69|median follow-up was 40 months.
70|Treatment
71|The median time from randomization to the ini-
72|tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
73|median time from the initiation of ADT to the
74|initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
75|tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
76|S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
77|patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
78|not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
79|clined treatment. The median duration of abira
80|terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
81|for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
82|(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
83|tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
84|continue through progression (51% reported per-
85|manent stopping for progression and 20% for
86|excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
87|the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
88|patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
89|treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
90|report.
91|The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
92|41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
93|alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
94|therapy was 39% in the combination group and
95|40% in the ADT-alone group.
96|Overall Survival
97|There were 184 deaths in the combination group
98|and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
99|strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
100|combination group, with a 3-year survival of
101|83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
102|group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
103|dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).
